hints: Start by picturing the path of an impulse through a motor neurone - where does it first arrive and where must it finally leave?
Think about which end has many short branched fibres to collect signals, and which end has one very long fibre to carry signals away.
Recall where the nucleus sits in a motor neurone and why that region needs a lot of energy and protein synthesis machinery.
Link structure to high metabolic demand - which two organelles would you expect to be abundant in the cell body?
Remember how a long axon is insulated in mammals and what gaps in that insulation are called.
Finish at the far tip of the axon - what small swellings allow the neurone to pass the message to a muscle?
walkthrough:
Receiving End - Dendrites and Cell Body**
Think of a motor neurone as having a receiving end and a transmitting end. Dendrites are short branched fibres that carry impulses toward the cell body. The cell body or soma contains the nucleus at one end of the cell.

Supporting a Busy Cell - Mitochondria and RER**
The cell body is metabolically very active because it makes neurotransmitter, ion channel proteins and maintains ion gradients. So you find many mitochondria for ATP and much rough endoplasmic reticulum, seen as Nissl's granules, for protein synthesis.

Transmitting End - Axon, Myelin and Synaptic Knobs**
There is one single long axon that carries the action potential away from the cell body toward the muscle. The axon is wrapped by Schwann cells forming the myelin sheath, with gaps called nodes of Ranvier. At the far end the axon branches to synaptic knobs or boutons that contact the effector.

Final answer: Motor neurone has dendrites leading to a cell body/soma containing the nucleus; cell body contains many mitochondria and much RER/Nissl's granules; has a single long axon; axon ends in synaptic knobs/termini/boutons; axon surrounded by Schwann cells/myelin sheath with nodes of Ranvier.

hints: Start from a resting axon at about -70 mV - what must change in membrane permeability to make the inside less negative?
Focus on which positive ion rushes in first and through what type of membrane protein it passes.
Think about what happens to the potential difference when that influx occurs, up to about +40 mV, and what this phase is called.
Consider how the membrane is reset - which channels now close and which different ion channels open?
Follow the second ion - which way does it move and how does that make the inside negative again?
Zoom out from one patch of membrane to the whole axon - how does one depolarised region trigger the next region?
Add myelin to the picture - as a fatty layer, what does it prevent across most of the axon membrane?
Use that idea to explain where an action potential can actually be regenerated in a myelinated neurone.
Put it together to name this fast node-to-node mode of transmission and state the direction it travels.
walkthrough:
Depolarisation - Sodium In**
At rest the inside is negative relative to the outside. When threshold is reached, voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels open. $Na^+$ diffuses rapidly into the axon down its electrochemical gradient. The inside becomes less negative, then positive to about +40 mV. This reversal is depolarisation.

Repolarisation - Sodium Stops, Potassium Out**
Almost immediately the $Na^+$ channels close and voltage-gated $K^+$ channels open. $K^+$ moves out of the cell. Loss of positive ions makes the inside negative again. This return is repolarisation, often with brief hyperpolarisation and a refractory period.

Local Circuits Move the Signal Along**
The influx of $Na^+$ in one region makes that region positive, so positive ions are attracted sideways to the adjacent resting negative region. This local circuit depolarises the next patch of membrane to threshold, opening its $Na^+$ channels. In this way the action potential is regenerated along the axon.

Myelin Makes It Saltatory and Fast**
Myelin made by Schwann cells is an electrical insulator. It prevents ion movement and depolarisation across myelinated regions. Voltage-gated channels are concentrated at nodes of Ranvier. So the action potential occurs only at nodes and appears to jump from node to node. This is saltatory conduction, which is much faster and travels in one unidirectional wave because the previous region is refractory.

Final answer: Voltage-gated $Na^+$ channels open, $Na^+$ enters axon causing depolarisation to about +40 mV; then $Na^+$ channels close and voltage-gated $K^+$ channels open, $K^+$ moves out causing repolarisation; depolarisation sets up local circuits; myelin/Schwann cells insulate axon preventing ion movement; action potential occurs only at nodes of Ranvier so impulse jumps node to node by saltatory conduction in one direction.
